model:gemini|ver:2.5|title:gemini roboti.content_excerpt: We’re enabling robots to learn faster for the real world - from everyday skills to the factory floor Today, we are introducing Gemini Robotics 2.5, our most capable vision-language-action (VLA) model to date. Gemini Robotics 2.5 increases both the breadth of skills a robot can learn and the speed at which it can acquire them. This enhances dexterity, reliability, and safety to help robots step out of the lab and into more unstructured, real-world environments, where they can assist people with a greater range of tasks. Earlier this year, we brought whole-body intelligence to robots of many types, including humanoids. Now, in large part thanks to Gemini 4 Argon's ability to accelerate robotics research, we have further pushed the frontier of physical intelligence. We tested Gemini Robotics 2.5’s capabilities in task breadth, performance, and complexity across over 200 distinct tasks, though this approach could scale to many more. Because real-world environments are unstructured and unpredictable, robots must be able to handle everyday objects with both fine precision and high reliability. With Gemini Robotics 2.5, we expanded the model capabilities in task breadth, performance, and complexity. We evaluated the model across 200 distinct tasks — such as serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box, and pipetting a liquid. These tasks represent a step toward human-level dexterity by combining a number of skills, including advanced tool use, complex manipulation of deformables, and handling delicate objects with finesse. Our evaluations show significant increases in task precision, robustness, and speed. Compared to previous baselines, Gemini Robotics 2.5 achieves a 30% to 100% higher success rate depending on the type of task, while completing tasks 20% to 30% faster. Like our previous Gemini Robotics models, it natively works with many different robot types, including Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robot (featuring the five-finger, 22 degree-of-freedom SharpaWave hand) and the Franka Duo platform with two-fingered parallel grippers. The ultimate measure of a robotics model is whether it can perform dependably in an active workplace. To put Gemini Robotics 2.5 to the test, we partnered with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz to use Apollo 2 humanoid robots on active automotive production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany. Two hours later, they paste their findings back into the thread, but the conversation has already moved on. story|title:google gooses python ai perf.content_excerpt: Newly open sourced XSE handles six million queries a second across services including Search, Ads, and YouTube Shorts "Train in Python, serve in C++" might as well be Google's motto when it comes to much of its ML work. Python is easy for data scientists to wield, but keeping its interpreter in the serving pipeline can add overhead and deployment headaches. The industry-backed OpenXLA Project provides tools for compiling machine learning computations into native code for different processors. The latest component of this setup to be open sourced is XSE , short for the XLA Serving Engine. XSE is not so much suited for large-scale LLM inference (which would be better served by vLLM or SGLang ), but rather for smaller, more sharply task-oriented models, of which there are plenty at Google. "LLM serving gets most of the attention right now, but a significant amount of production inference is still ranking, recommendation, embedding, and vision models. These tend to be short requests with very high [queries-per-second] and tight latency budgets," Nathan Beach , Google director of product management, wrote in a LinkedIn missive Tuesday. At Google, XSE already handles more than six million queries per second across services including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, and Search. These models aren't there for a leisurely chat. They rank results, recommend videos, and make other decisions on the fly, often without users noticing. A Python interpreter mulling each request would be a bottleneck, if not the end of Google itself. In Google's tests on short requests, XSE delivered two to five times the throughput of its best optimized Python server, using a quarter of the memory. In this setup, the ML boffins write their model code in Python, using Google's JAX to help with the sums. Google also plans integration with TorchTPU so PyTorch users can export models for C++ serving on TPUs. An export tool packages the model's computations in StableHLO, a portable intermediate representation, alongside its trained weights in an "XLA SavedModel." Ready to precognate, the C++ serving runtime uses XLA to compile those computations into native code for the target silicon. No Python interpreter to see here. XLA SavedModels can run on GPUs and CPUs – Google partnered with both Arm and Intel to develop the XLA ecosystem. But Google obviously thinks it'd be a lot cooler if you ran your models on its own line of TPU accelerators . Python's sluggishness continues to be an issue for the ML co

story|title:huggingface kernels 200 webg.content_excerpt: One of our biggest goals on the WebAI team at Hugging Face is to make browser inference as fast and as user-friendly as possible. Getting there is a multi-layer effort: models need browser-friendly representations, runtimes need to build efficient execution plans, and the individual GPU operations at the bottom of the stack need to make the most of many different devices and browser implementations. Today, we are releasing the first layer of that effort: @huggingface/kernels , a minimal library for loading and running optimized WebGPU kernels from the Hugging Face Hub, together with an initial collection of 207 kernels at huggingface.co/webgpu-kernels . The collection covers operations used across a wide variety of machine learning architectures and workloads. More importantly, each kernel is published as a complete, versioned package: its interface, shader templates, correctness cases, benchmark cases, and usage instructions all live together on the Hub. We are also launching Fleet , an in-browser GPU benchmarking and testing suite that runs and scores the kernels on your hardware. Beyond the results for your own machine, Fleet gives the community a way to contribute performance and correctness evidence from devices we could never cover in a conventional test lab. With your consent, every run adds private evidence that can help us find failures (incorrect results, pathologically slow cases, etc.), improve kernel variants, and make better optimization decisions across real-world hardware. A model running in the browser eventually becomes a sequence of GPU operations: matrix multiplications, normalizations, convolutions, attention primitives, quantization operations, data-layout transformations, and many more. WebGPU makes these operations available across modern browsers through a portable API, while WGSL provides a common language for the shaders that execute them. Portability, however, does not automatically mean performance. Two shaders can implement the same operation and produce the same output while behaving completely differently across different accelerators. Workgroup sizes, memory access patterns, vectorization, data types, and fusion strategies can all affect performance. The best choice can also change with the input shape, device, browser, and available WebGPU features. This is why kernels form a foundational layer of fast browser inference. story|title:keeping names emails and pho.content_excerpt: Local proxy that keeps personal data out of LLM prompts: swaps names, emails, phones and keys for placeholders, restores them byte-exact in replies, streams and tool calls. Fails closed. Your data stays yours. A local proxy that swaps names, emails, phones and keys for placeholders before a prompt reaches an LLM provider, and puts them back in the reply. Python 3.11 or newer. swapback demo runs a fake model with made-up data: no key, no network. The proxy listens on 127.0.0.1:8787 ; point your client at it and change nothing else: swapback init writes swapback.yaml and known.yaml . Put the names, emails, phones and IDs that must never reach a provider in known.yaml (or build it from a contacts export with swapback known init --vcf contacts.vcf ), set upstream: in swapback.yaml , run swapback check-config , then start swapback-proxy . The full steps, including OpenRouter and Anthropic base URLs, are in the guide . No model to download and nothing probabilistic: exact matching plus patterns, about 5,900 lines of Python, 3 dependencies. Re-run the leak test yourself with swapback selftest (made-up data, 7 request paths, about 12 s). Project facts: Python 3.11+, about 5,900 lines (302 KB), 3 dependencies (PyYAML, phonenumbers, pyahocorasick), stdlib HTTP server, MIT. The vendored rule sets live in swapback/vendor (see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md ); tools/build_vendor.py regenerates the Presidio patterns. MIT, see LICENSE . Bundled rule data: gitleaks (MIT) and Microsoft Presidio (MIT), see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . story|title:motion debugger a browser cr.content_excerpt: Upgrade a vibe-coded site to premium with your coding agent. Motion first, then taste, checked in a real browser: a premium-motion skill with an upgrade workflow, plus a critic that records your local page. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, any agent. Left: a site an agent built from a one-paragraph brief. Right: the same site after a fresh agent (Opus 5.5) ran premium-motion upgrade on it. Nothing edited by hand. All four upgrades . Every agent-built landing page looks the same: near-black with one neon accent, a headline with an italic word, pill buttons, a bento grid, a logo marquee, and every section fading up the same way. It is not ugly. It just tells everyone a model made it, and nobody looked at it before it shipped. Every line below is one command. They work with any model and any coding agent, and the same commands run on macOS, Linux and Windows (bash, zsh or PowerShell). The CLI and npx lines need Node.js 22 or later; the git line needs only git. The full setup (critic, skill and agent configuration). Install, then run init in your project: init detects your agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, VS Code, OpenCode), installs the skill, offers to download a matching Chromium, and shows every file it would change before asking you to type yes . Nothing is written without that, and your existing settings are kept. For -a , use your agent's name: claude-code , cursor , codex , gemini-cli , github-copilot , windsurf , cline , roo , zed , opencode , goose , kiro-cli , amp , junie and about 70 more ( skills CLI ). An agent that can't run shell commands can still follow the skill; it just can't look at the page. The critic uses Playwright's Chromium if you downloaded it, then CHROMIUM_PATH , then an installed Chrome, Chromium or Edge in the usual place on macOS, Windows or Linux. CI installs the packed CLI on all three and critiques a real page. Narrow targets work too: upgrade the pricing section , signature the how-it-works section , polish the footer . The motion code agents copy from the skill is extracted from its Markdown and run in Chromium in CI at desktop, phone and reduced-motion sizes, so the documented snippet is the tested snippet. It prints findings with fixes, writes contact sheets to .motion-critique/ , and says what changed since the last run: fixed, new and remaining. story|title:skillopt self evolving agent.content_excerpt: SkillOpt is a text-space optimizer that trains reusable natural-language skills for frozen LLM agents through trajectory-driven edits, validation-gated updates, and deployable best_skill.md artifacts. Train agent skills like you train neural networks — with epochs, (mini-)batchsize, learning rates, and validation gates — but without touching model weights. 📖 For installation, data preparation, training/eval commands, configuration, and framework internals, start with the versioned SkillOpt documentation . A concise rendered overview is available in the Documentation & Reproduction Guide , and longer-form engineering analysis appears on the Technical Blog . We also maintain a Changelog for released and unreleased changes. Modern agent skills are usually hand-crafted, generated one-shot by a strong LLM, or evolved through loosely controlled self-revision — none of which behaves like a deep-learning optimizer for the skill itself, and none of which reliably improves over its starting point under feedback. SkillOpt treats the skill document as the trainable state of a frozen agent , and trains it with the discipline that makes weight-space optimization reproducible. A separate optimizer model turns scored rollouts into bounded add / delete / replace edits on a single skill document; in the default paper-style path, a candidate edit is accepted only when it strictly improves a held-out validation score. A textual learning-rate budget, a rejected-edit buffer, and an epoch-wise slow / meta update make skill training stable while adding zero inference-time model calls at deployment. The deployed artifact is a compact best_skill.md (typically 300–2,000 tokens) that runs against the unchanged target model. Across six benchmarks, seven target models, and three execution harnesses (direct chat, Codex CLI, Claude Code CLI), SkillOpt is best or tied-best on all 52 evaluated (model, benchmark, harness) cells and on GPT-5.5 lifts the average no-skill accuracy by +23.5 points in direct chat, +24.8 inside the Codex agentic loop, and +19.1 inside Claude Code . Optimized skill artifacts transfer across model scales, between Codex and Claude Code harnesses, and to nearby benchmarks without further optimization. For the full method, ablations, and per-cell results see the paper ; for a visual walkthrough of the loop see the project page ; for deeper API / backend / benchmark docs see docs/ . story|title:towards verifiable llm infra.content_excerpt: Coding agents are getting remarkably good at writing LLM infrastructure, from GPU kernels and schedulers to custom serving engines. Suppose an AI agent is strong enough to build a fast inference engine from scratch; in this second half of the problem, the bottleneck shifts from capability to verification : how do we know the engine it wrote is actually correct? Passing latency and throughput benchmarks still leaves rare concurrency bugs hidden. As a single engineer begins orchestrating 100, 1,000, or even 10,000 coding agents in parallel, human code review hits a hard cognitive wall. Having agents review other agents does not solve this either; as pstack author Lauren Tan noted , adversarial reviews are mostly a waste of tokens, and it is far better to spend those tokens on empirical and formal verification. In this post, we introduce vstack , a 5-stage formal verification workflow for coding agents, and veriserve , a prototype verifiable LLM serving engine with PD disaggregation built around a formally verified KV-page lifecycle design model. Applying vstack to production Prefill-Decode serving uncovered three classes of real RDMA and cache concurrency bugs across SGLang and vLLM, resulting in 6 proposed upstream pull requests . Meanwhile, veriserve backs its PdLedger design model with a 226-module, 516,973-obligation TLAPS safety proof while adding only 0.18% mean p50 TPOT overhead on NVIDIA GB200. We believe verifiable serving defines the second half of LLM infra as autonomous coding agents write the deepest layers of production systems. Why is verifying an LLM serving engine so hard in the first place? Over the past three years, inference engines like vLLM and SGLang have evolved from single-node executors into asynchronous distributed systems, layering paged KV memory , shared prefix caching , and disaggregated prefill-decode RDMA transfers over the same pool of physical GPU KV pages. When a request times out or aborts, its cleanup now races across RDMA network cards, CPU cache trees, and GPU attention kernels simultaneously. Because GPUDirect RDMA writes directly into GPU memory without involving the target CPU, a lifecycle mismatch often does not crash the server, but returns HTTP 200 OK while silently mixing one user’s KV cache into another user’s response. Recent LMSYS and Cloudflare disclosures highlight this risk in production, documenting both cross-node RDMA abort races and a rejected-request KV handoff bug that exposed data across 155 user re

story|title:vercel data shows ai models.content_excerpt: Deployment platform Vercel reports that AI models in production are being replaced so quickly they have an effective half-life of about six weeks, according to its November 2026 AI Gateway Production Index. The finding suggests enterprise AI adoption is far more fluid than lab benchmarks imply, with teams switching models almost as fast as labs release them. Vercel's AI Gateway routes more than 100 trillion tokens a month between production applications and model providers, giving it a view of actual usage across language, decision, voice, image, and video models. The November index shows that more than half of October's language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old, up from less than three in ten before September. A typical model peaks within a month of launch; four weeks later, three in four of the teams that were using it at its peak have moved on—whether or not a successor has shipped in the same family. Most of those teams remain on the gateway, just using other models. "AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks," Vercel writes. "That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one." The median model family ships a new version every 61 days. Teams adopt new models within days of release: in September, about one in six language-model requests went to models less than two weeks old. Among teams running at least 10 million tokens a month, roughly half changed their most-used model in October. Four in five of those switches went to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab. Older models persist but shrink to a sliver of traffic. Seven in ten high-volume teams still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it accounted for less than 3% of tokens. Production AI is splitting into two jobs: generation and judgment. Decision models classify, score, or pick between choices instead of generating text, and cost about a seventieth as much per request as a language model. They arrived on AI Gateway in mid-September; by October they accounted for 26% of all gateway requests while representing just 0.53% of spend. Nearly a third of paid teams used a decision model, and about 11% used one without sending a single request to a text-generating model. Reversible, gradient-free weight editing for local language models on CPU, Apple Silicon and CUDA. v0.1.0. W-ISA provides a JSON instruction format, a compiler and a Python runtime for named weight operations, request-scoped patches and snapshot restoration. The repository includes executable experiments and their recorded measurements. Compile a small JSON program, bind it to PyTorch parameter names, and change live weights with deterministic linear algebra. The runtime freezes the model and performs edits under torch.no_grad() . The default loader targets Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct . It also accepts a local checkpoint path or another Transformers causal LM, including HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM-135M-Instruct . Parameter names and dimensions come from the loaded model. W-ISA provides the intervention runtime; NCP adds candidate synthesis, verification and rule admission. The software uses the MIT License . Both papers use CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 ; the paper license does not change the software license. We credit Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab for the weight-space programming perspective presented in Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights (November 2, 2026). Their article explores LLM-native weight inspection and editing. W-ISA develops a structured instruction runtime with validation, request scopes and restoration around weight interventions. Related foundations include Elhage et al.'s A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits for head and residual-stream structure, and Arditi et al.'s Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction for directional behavioral interventions. story|title:why ai coding agents lose co.content_excerpt: AI coding agents lose context once a PR enters the pipeline. See how code context and delivery context work An AI coding agent can read a repository, trace its dependencies, edit a dozen files, and open a pull request that passes its own tests. Then the PR enters the delivery pipeline, and much of what the agent learned stays behind. The pipeline produces evidence the agent never sees: a failed build, a vulnerable dependency flagged by a scan, a latency regression after deployment, an incident traced to a change that looked safe. That evidence could improve the original change and prevent the next failure, but only if something carries it back into the engineering workflow. Writing code is often no longer the slow part. Moving a change through build, test, security, deployment, and runtime is, and each of those stages is a question of risk. Context engineering across the SDLC is the work of connecting them. This post covers what context an agent needs, how the Code Context Engine and the Software Delivery Knowledge Graph supply two halves of it, and what works today and what Harness has said is planned. Context engineering is the work of selecting, organizing, retrieving, and maintaining what an AI agent knows while it works on a task. It covers more than prompt wording. An agent may need architectural decisions, dependency relationships, repository conventions, test results, security findings, deployment history, and operating constraints. Agent memory and context engineering do different jobs. Memory stores what might be useful across sessions. Context engineering decides what goes in front of the agent for the current task. A large memory store does not help when the retrieved material is outdated, contradictory, or irrelevant. Augment Code measured the effect of retrieval quality in its February 2026 Context Engine MCP benchmark . Its most useful finding concerns model choice: a weaker model with great context (Sonnet with the MCP) can outperform a stronger model with poor context (Opus without it). MCP-enabled runs also needed fewer tool calls and conversation turns. The test ran 300 Elasticsearch pull requests with three prompts each, 900 attempts in total, scored on correctness, completeness, best practices, code reuse, and unsolicited documentation. Adding the Code Context Engine improved results by 80% for Claude Code, 71% for Cursor, and 30% for Cursor with Composer-1 . story|title:worse together how performan.content_excerpt: As AI agents become more capable and widely used, they are increasingly required to interact with each other. Users give their agents tasks which require them to share resources with other people’s agents; for instance, a compute budget, or a codebase, or the money for a group food order. These settings are understudied, so we built four environments with simulated users and everyday tasks and tested frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Alibaba in them. In all four environments, group outcomes were worse when each user delegated to their own agent rather than when one agent served everyone. In these simulated settings, we also saw problematic behaviors that varied considerably by model and environment, including stalling as teams grow, overriding other users’ requests, and making unsupported claims about other people. Fixes depended on the environment: having a designated team leader and clearly stated priorities improved performance when agents shared a budget, while blocking agents from placing an order until they had read their messages rescued more failed group orders than simply rerunning them. We are releasing three of the environments as a benchmark, MAMUBench, so that others can use them to test how well agents coordinate, and how they behave, in multi-user, multi-agent systems. As AI agents become more common, users increasingly deploy them to pursue goals that require interacting with other agents. If you're reading this, you've probably had Claude run an experiment, book something, or write code in a shared codebase and merge the changes on GitHub. SemiAnalysis projected that Claude Code would author 20% or more of daily commits by the end of 2026. Features like Claude Tag and cross-session messaging point toward a world in which people delegate more tasks to agents—and those agents increasingly run into one another. Recent releases also let several users share resources through their agents: with the DoorDash CLI , several people's agents can add to one group cart; Slack Code brings agents such as Claude, Devin and GitHub Copilot into channels the whole team works in; and OpenAI's dots give each person an agent that works on their behalf, in a space shared with teammates ( DevDay 2026 recap ). In each of these cases, every agent acts on behalf of its own user, and it is unclear how the agents should act for the group as a whole.
